newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN INTERIOR MINISTER NOMINATED AS PREMIER.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN INTERIOR MINISTER NOMINATED AS PREMIER.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Tuesday nominated powerful Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev as prime minister to head Bulgaria's ninth government since the end of one-party rule in 1989.
If his nomination is approved, Dobrev will form a new cabinet in the coming days to tackle the country's grave economic crisis.

A Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) spokeswoman said Dobrev's nomination had first to be approved by the Socialists' parliamentary allies and then voted in parliament, where the ruling party has a majority.
"Dobrev was the only politician in the Socialist government who met the approval of all political forces," said Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics.

Dobrev was responsible for human resources issues in the BSP for several years and became interior minister in May after his predecessor Lyubomir Nachev was dismissed for failing to deal with escalating crime.

He is perceived as one of the party's strongmen due to the great access to information provided by his posts, political analysts say. Bulgarian police files from the communist era have never been made public as they were in East Germany.

"There are many deputies with strong business interests in the BSP and other parliamentary groups who fear that a strong figure like Dobrev will be in a position to stop the abuse of power for private business interests," said Stanchev.
Parliament is expected to vote later this week.
"It is likely that Dobrev will past the vote by a narrow margin, as many deputies have reasons to prefer a weaker figure for a prime minister," said Stanchev.
After months of criticism of his handling of the economy, Zhan Videnov resigned as premier and party leader at a party congress on December 21, sparking a showdown between hardliners and reformists.

Dobrev, 49, emerged as an outspoken critic of Videnov at the congress, where he attacked the cabinet's record in handling the country's economic and social crisis and raised the previously taboo issue of government corruption.
A mining engineer by training, Dobrev was a leader of the Communist youth organisation Komsomol before 1989. He has also chaired parliament's national security committee.
Critics of his candidature say he lacks the economic expertise necessary to win the approval of Bulgaria's foreign partners.

International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials have said that once a new government is formed they are prepared to complete talks on implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime proposed as a last resort to restore confidence in the crumbling financial system.

Two IMF missions visited Bulgaria in December to help the government and the central bank prepare the introduction of a currency board, which is expected to halt the collapse of the national currency and curb inflation.
One of the first tasks of the new government may be to redraft the 1997 budget. Economists criticised the draft introduced to parliament by Videnov last week for unrealistic assumptions.
The opposition says the Socialists, who are half way through their parliamentary term, no longer have the pubic support to govern and fresh elections should be held.

They have organised protest rallies outside the Socialist party headquarters in Sofia and in other major cities in the past few days demanding early elections. More rallies are planned later in the week.
